summary: Describes UTF-8, a way to encode the characters of ISO 10646 that keeps the US-ASCII range unchanged, so software that expects ASCII keeps working. It replaces RFC 2044 and was replaced by RFC 3629.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a way to write every language's letters using bytes. English letters stay the same as old systems, so old programs still work.

questions: how many bytes is a utf-8 character
subtitle: A variable-length way to write every ISO 10646 character in bytes while leaving plain ASCII untouched.

tldr.problem: Multi-octet character encodings such as UCS-2 and UCS-4 do not work with many applications and protocols that expect 7 or 8 bit characters.
tldr.mechanism: UTF-8 encodes each character as 1 to 6 octets. ASCII characters keep their single-octet values, and the first octet of longer sequences tells how many octets follow.
tldr.outcome: Plain ASCII is already valid UTF-8 and ASCII bytes never appear inside other characters. RFC 2279 replaced RFC 2044 and has itself been obsoleted by RFC 3629.

today: RFC 2279 replaced RFC 2044, was a Draft Standard, and has since been obsoleted by RFC 3629, which is the current UTF-8 specification.

sections.title: Why UTF-8 Exists
sections.content:
ISO/IEC 10646-1 defines the Universal Character Set (UCS), covering most of the world's writing systems. It has a four-octet encoding, UCS-4, and a two-octet encoding, UCS-2, which can address only the first 64K characters (the Basic Multilingual Plane). Both are hard to use with software that assumes 7 or 8 bit characters.

The answer was a family of UCS transformation formats. UTF-8 uses all bits of an octet but preserves the full US-ASCII range: ASCII characters are one octet with their normal value, and any octet with such a value can only stand for an ASCII character. UTF-7 uses only 7-bit values, and UTF-1 is of historical interest only.

The RFC lists other properties: the first octet of a multi-octet sequence gives its length, the octet values FE and FF never appear, character boundaries are easy to find from anywhere in a stream, the sort order of UCS-4 strings is preserved, and valid UTF-8 is unlikely to be mistaken for another encoding.
sections.plainLanguage: UTF-8 lets computers write every language's letters using ordinary bytes, while English letters look exactly like they always did.

sections.title: The UTF-8 Byte Patterns
sections.content:
Characters become sequences of 1 to 6 octets. A single-octet sequence starts with a 0 bit and carries 7 bits of the value. In a sequence of n octets with n greater than 1, the first octet starts with n bits set to 1 and then a 0. Every following octet starts with the bits 10 and holds 6 bits of the value.

To encode, pick the row of the table that fits the character value (the rows are mutually exclusive, so there is only one valid encoding), set the leading bits, and fill the x positions from the low-order bits of the value, starting at the last octet. Decoding runs the same steps backwards. UCS-2 surrogate pairs between D800 and DFFF come from UTF-16 and must be converted back to a UCS-4 character before encoding.

Decoders must guard against invalid sequences. A naive one may decode the invalid sequence C0 80 as U+0000, which can have security consequences.
sections.plainLanguage: The first byte says how long the letter is, like a label saying this takes three boxes. Each extra box is stamped so you can tell it is a continuation.

sections.title: Versions and the Korean Mess
sections.content:
ISO/IEC 10646 and Unicode are updated over time. Usually that only adds characters, which is harmless to old data. Amendment 5 to ISO/IEC 10646 is different: it moved and expanded the Korean Hangul block, making earlier Hangul data invalid. Unicode 2.0 has the same difference from Unicode 1.1.

The justification was that no implementations or data containing Hangul existed. The incident became known as the Korean mess, and the committees pledged never to make such an incompatible change again.
sections.plainLanguage: Once, the people who keep the character list rearranged the Korean letters and old files stopped matching. They promised never to do that again.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives three examples. The UCS-2 sequence for A, NOT IDENTICAL TO, ALPHA and a full stop (0041, 2262, 0391, 002E) becomes 41 E2 89 A2 CE 91 2E. The Korean word hangugo (D55C, AD6D, C5B4) becomes ED 95 9C EA B5 AD EC 96 B4. The Japanese word nihongo (65E5, 672C, 8A9E) becomes E6 97 A5 E6 9C AC E8 AA 9E.

Note how A and the full stop stay as the single octets 41 and 2E, while the other characters take two or three octets.
sections.plainLanguage: The letter A takes one byte, as always. A Korean or Japanese character takes three bytes.

sections.title: The MIME Charset Label
sections.content:
The memo is meant as the basis for registering the MIME charset value UTF-8, suitable for the text top-level type. The label deliberately has no version number. Version-specific labels would make older applications fail to recognize newer ones, while a generic label gives mostly correct processing.

The Korean mess is an incompatible change, so the label is understood to cover all versions after Amendment 5. A second value, UNICODE-1-1-UTF-8, is proposed only for Hangul text encoded before Amendment 5. Other UTF-8 data SHOULD NOT use it.
sections.plainLanguage: The tag on the data just says UTF-8, with no version, so old programs still recognize it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Implementors need to think about how they treat illegal UTF-8 sequences, because an attacker may exploit an incautious parser. A subtle attack targets a parser that checks the UTF-8 form of its input for forbidden content but later interprets some illegal sequences as characters.

The RFC's examples: a parser might forbid the NUL character as the single octet 00 yet accept the illegal two-octet C0 80 as NUL. Another might forbid 2F 2E 2E 2F (the string /../) but permit the illegal 2F C0 AE 2E 2F.
sections.plainLanguage: A sneaky sender might write a forbidden letter in a disguised, longer way. Programs must reject the disguises.
